entry.title: Friday Storm Update: Trending Colder
entry.content:
Friday AM update: The forecast models trended a little colder overnight. Rain this morning will turn to snow in the mountains by this afternoon and in town by late afternoon or early evening. With the colder air arriving a bit earlier, totals should land toward the upper end of (or slightly above) the 2–4"+ for Bridger and 4–8"+ for Big Sky from the forecast earlier this week.

Radar this morning with airport temperatures and winds; the cold front (blue line) is moving in from the west

In Bozeman, it'll be mostly rain during the day, but by late afternoon – early evening, colder air filtering in plus heavy precipitation rates should lead to a snow changeover. Slick spots are definitely possible for the evening commute, and things could get a little dicey around Bozeman Pass and up the canyon toward Big Sky. FYI, the NWS has a Winter Weather Advisory for the Gallatin and Madison mountains from noon to midnight.

HRRR forecast, 6 AM–9 PM Friday

entry.title: An October Surprise? Rain or Snow?
entry.content:
Since the storm potential I mentioned late last week is now closer on the horizon, I'll provide a few more details with a rundown of the latest model guidance. The storm system is already taking shape off the Pacific coast and will first impact the Southwest U.S. beginning tomorrow into Thursday. There's actually a decent shot of a somewhat rare severe thunderstorm threat across parts of Southern California, Arizona, and Southern Utah with the SPC issuing a Day 2 enhanced risk outlook centered over Arizona: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/. This is the kind of southern-track storm that El Niño tends to favor. You can go back and see our first post ever that talked a bit about the southern storm track: https://coldsmokereport.com/posts/el-nino-and-bridger-bowl-record-winter/.

Below is today's latest GFS model forecast for Thursday into Saturday. The upper-level low and trough across the Pacific coast and Southwest will move northeast towards our region, bringing with it an increased chance of rain beginning Thursday night.

Also, just FYI, the rain/snow colors above are from the GFS's coarse 0.25° grid. The model's coarse resolution means it resolves the mountains only as a block averaged across 25 km, which mutes the actual prominence and elevation of the narrow Bridger range. Consequently, the cells around Bridger are actually closer to valley elevation in the model. The forecast is still mountain snow in the late afternoon - evening.

The heaviest precipitation will move across the region Friday during the day and into Friday evening. This is one of the rare situations where I'm actually rooting for rain at higher elevations to start. I haven't had a chance to go up and look myself, but I've been concerned about snowfall from the other week faceting on high-elevation, north-facing aspects that get very little sun this time of year. It may get warm enough the next couple of days regardless, but I'd rather be safe than sorry. By Friday PM, rain should change over to snow, heavy at times for the higher elevations. This storm might favor Big Sky a little bit more than the Bridgers due to high initial snow levels.

What are we looking at for totals? Both the GFS and European model ensembles are showing 0.5–1.5" of liquid water equivalent. A lot will come down to how quickly the colder air can filter in but right now I think 4–8+ inches of snow at the upper mountain of Big Sky is a decent possibility.

For Bridger, due to the storm being a bit on the warmer side initially, I'd expect totals to likely be a bit lower, more towards 2–4"+ with higher amounts possible near the ridge.

What about town? Expect mostly rain in Bozeman Friday, around 0.5–1". The cold air arrives as the moisture is moving out, so snow levels likely won't reach the valley floor until things are close to winding down late Friday night. If the moisture hangs around longer, a slushy coating Saturday morning is possible, but I'm not expecting much. (Yes, I remember last time 🙃. I'll be watching the high-resolution models for any sign of the cold air arriving early.)

I'll keep you all updated as the storm gets within range of the higher-resolution short range models. Thanks for checking in!

-Trey

entry.title: When should I do my winter tire swap?
entry.content:
After last weekend's storm, we're quickly thawing out and it looks like beautiful weather for this weekend. Hope you all are able to get out and enjoy it! The topic of today's post is something I've seen floating around the interwebs and a common question around town this time of year: When should I do my winter tire swap? I'm going to try to answer this with a bit of science and the latest weather forecasts.

We technically already had our first snowfall, with some road accumulation, in the last storm. However, road conditions only seemed dicey for maybe ~12-18 hours during the worst of the snow late Sun - early Mon. For those that held out and haven't swapped yet, you will be rewarded :). More on that in a bit. I should also add a couple of caveats here that may affect decision making. If you have to commute over a higher-elevation pass like Bozeman Pass, for instance, that probably bumps up these timelines a bit. Also, a lot likely depends on the traction quality of your current tire set. If you already have decent All-season tires, that allows for more risk tolerance. Okay, let's get into the #s!

For the Oct 10–12 storm you can see that we were right at the typical date for the first snowfall, but about 10 days ahead of schedule for the first 1-inch snowfall. Week-average highs dropping below 45ºF is used here as a rough threshold for when snow starts sticking to roads more easily, since colder road surfaces collect snow more effectively. Typically early November is when those temperatures are consistently colder.

Another consideration is the number of "warm days" left (from both a climatological and forecast standpoint). Basically, with the warmer weather that's expected over the next 5–7 days, we're still expecting another 10+ days with highs over 60ºF for the remainder of this year. More than half of these are this next week. With this information, if you're able to hold out, waiting at least another week, maybe 2 would prevent you from driving on warmer roads (and potentially wearing down your tires a bit faster). If you're not driving a lot, it's probably no biggie, but if you are, it's worth factoring in, in addition to increased fuel costs if you swap to winter tires too early. Overall, my recommendation would be the last week of October or first week of November for those that mostly do in town driving. For those with more mountain driving (or current tires aren't great), I'd recommend changing them out here sometime in the next week.

Finally, looking at the current forecast, it's likely we'll be above average in terms of temperatures for the next ~week before we may see our next storm system late next week. The next chance for colder weather and any potential snow looks to be Thursday night through Saturday (Oct 22–24). There’s a lot of uncertainty with the models right now: ECMWF and its ensembles are more aggressive, showing a 72% chance of >0.25” of water (44% chance of at least .25” falling as snow, which would be 2-3” in the Bridgers). The GFS ensembles, on the other hand, only show a 32% (16%) probability of decent precipitation. For those that aren't familiar with ensembles, I'll leave the details for a future post but they're essentially a model that's run with several slightly different combinations of either the initial state or model parameters. This is done because we know there are deficiencies in both the model and characterization of the initial atmosphere (a model's starting point). This allows us to get a more realistic spread of potential outcomes.

We’ll keep an eye on things heading into early next week as the forecast evolves. Hope everyone has a great weekend!

-Trey

entry.title: Snow Day!
entry.content:
What a beautiful morning looking up at the ridge! Overall, snowfall totals in the Bridgers hit on the upper end of forecasted ranges with 10–14" at mid-upper elevations and 1.5–2" of liquid water equivalent. Totals at Big Sky were a bit lower (4–7"), highlighting the very tight gradients of precipitation that made this forecast particularly tricky. The forecast in town was definitely a bust to the upside with 4–8" of snow. What happened? In my previous post you can see the stalled frontal boundary draped across the valley on Saturday. It pushed just far enough south to allow colder air to filter in about 18 hours earlier than was forecasted. Furthermore, the snow stuck better to the warm ground than expected. Hopefully you escaped any tree damage, since most of the in-town foliage has yet to fall.

If you want to try to get a couple of turns in, I think low-angle grassy slopes may work (tips up and rock skis only!) in the Bridgers with the high water content. You'll need to get after it today, though. Looking ahead, temperatures will be a bit below average for the next couple of days before we rapidly warm up into late week. Mid-60s by the weekend means most of the low-mid elevation snow won't last. At the upper elevations (especially north-facing) we're going to keep a wary eye out for faceting and the potential for a weak layer near the ground if we don't quickly either fully melt (hard to do this time of year but not impossible) or continue to get additional snowfall. Keep an eye on https://www.mtavalanche.com/ for updated backcountry forecasts. Thanks for reading!

-Trey

entry.title: Incoming
entry.content:
Hope you all were able to get outside the past few days with the great fall weather we've had! I was able to get in one last bike ride this afternoon (huge shoutout to SWMMBA, Crosscut, and Bridger for the awesome new trails up there!).

Hopefully this will all be covered in snow the next time we see it :)

Radar, temperatures and winds from this afternoon (the front's position is from 3 PM):

Currently a stalled frontal boundary is draped across SW Montana as two storm systems converge over the region: One from the west/northwest and the other, associated with Tropical Storm Rachel to the south. Precipitation should transition to snow at upper elevation sites overnight Saturday, and overall the forecast still looks to be on track, 6–12"+ above mid-mountain. The heaviest snow looks to fall Sunday afternoon through Monday morning. In Bozeman, expect 1–3"+ by Monday morning, with the heaviest snow Sunday PM into the overnight. There is still some uncertainty and a fairly strong gradient of moisture and precipitation, so there could be some big winners and losers. Do your snow dances!

The HRRR model's forecast of Rachel's moisture plume through Monday midday (star = Bridger Bowl):

entry.title: Weekend Snow
entry.content:
Thanks, all, for the warm reception to the launch of this blog! It makes me excited that so many in our community are interested in the weather. Today’s post will cover this weekend’s potential storm. ❄️ ⛷🏂

It’s hard to believe with how warm it’s been over this past week (we’re just a few degrees shy of record highs for the date), but we may be talking about the potential for enough snow to ski early next week (at least for those with rock skis and flexible ACLs). Wait, what? Skiing already? Let me start off by saying that this is a very complex forecast. Why? We have a traditional frontal / mid-latitude storm system moving in from the west, but it’ll also be interacting with Hurricane Rachel that will be moving northward from the eastern Pacific. 

On Saturday PM a strong cold front will move through bringing heavy mountain precipitation that should quickly transition to snow at all elevations. Both the ECMWF (European weather model) and Google DeepMind (AI model) are trending more bullish with potential snowfall. Below is UofUtah’s downscaled snow ensemble (meaning it uses the large global GFS and ECMWF models and tries to “downscale” or extrapolate what precipitation might look like on smaller scales due to terrain effects, etc.). The GEFS and ECMWF ensembles in the Utah Snow Ensemble graphics below both show a mean of > 1" of water content. For early season storms we generally want more water content (less cold smoke) to help build our base. 

In the plots above you can see that both the GEFS and ECMWF ensembles are generally in decent agreement with the water content but less so on overall snowfall amounts. This is because the GEFS is quite a bit warmer than the ECMWF ensembles. Though I can’t completely discount that solution, it seems like it’s more of an outlier and I’d maybe lean towards the colder solutions with more snowfall based on current guidance.

With this, my current expectations would be 6–12”+ for the upper mountains at Bridger and Big Sky. Also, I think there's a decent likelihood of our first in-town snow in Bozeman overnight Saturday. Note that the IFS and GFS operational runs keep things a bit warmer and drier, which would make these totals lower. At this time, though, those models seem to be outliers. There's a pretty strong precipitation gradient from northwest - southeast that I'm keeping an eye on as well. I’ll also add that this is a quite complex forecast due to the interactions of multiple features here. Furthermore, I’d expect decreased predictability overall in the upcoming pattern for the next 2+ weeks. A former professor of mine writes a very interesting Utah-based blog (also helps run weather.utah.edu, where I got the plume graphic from) with a recent post on how western Pacific typhoons may be affecting the pattern downstream over the Intermountain West: https://wasatchweatherweenies.blogspot.com/2026/10/how-to-break-jet-stream.html.

And for the hardcore weather nerds: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/2015GL065082

Thanks for reading!

-Trey

P.S. for our friends farther west near Missoula and the Bitterroots, totals look a bit lighter.

entry.title: Welcome & What does El Niño mean for our Snow?
entry.content:
Hi all, welcome to the Cold Smoke Report! As an atmospheric scientist with a passion for skiing and snow, I've realized over the past few years that Southwest Montana is lacking a dedicated blog/site for snowfall forecasts. To start things off I'll be focusing on winter weather forecasts right here in the backyard at Bridger Bowl, Big Sky, and in Bozeman. Before I start with my first topic I've got a few ground rules and things I can promise for you all:

1) All forecasts will be written by a human, me. The full model/forecast and AI disclosure can be found on the "About" tab.

2) I will be wrong at times.

3) There are no bad questions, ask away.

4) This will always be a free community based resource.

5) I'll try to update as much as possible but can only promise a few posts per week during the season given the amount of time it takes to put together.

6) Oh and “Super” El Niño does not exist, scientifically speaking; I know it's semantics in terms of terminology but just so you all know :)

More than anything, though, I’m hoping this can be an educational resource for our community to better understand weather and science in general, including myself. With that, let's get into it!

I've probably either gotten the question or heard at least a hundred times this summer and fall, what does this El Niño mean for our snowfall? I thought that this will make for a good first post.

Unless you've been living under a rock, most folks know already that a record-strength El Niño is taking shape in the Pacific. As of the Climate Prediction Center's (CPC) late Sept. discussion, the ocean's still getting hotter with the key Niño-3.4 region sitting at +2.2 °C, and the eastern Pacific already past +3 °C. The CPC now has a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event, and, a 75% chance of a historic one, exceeding the strength of any El Niño back to 1950.

So the question for anyone with a Bridger or Big Sky pass: what does a big El Niño actually do to our snowfall in this region? To dig a little deeper I aggregated 76 seasons of SNOTEL recorded data along with the CPC's Oceanic Niño Index. TLDR: El Niño historically tilts the odds against us.

The snowfall totals in this post come from the nearest Bridger Bowl SNOTEL record (Brackett Creek) that extends back to 1950 after including the nearby co-op station. I'm using the daily change in snow depth, measured once a day after the snow has settled. Bridger's snow report that most are familiar with almost always measures higher (typically by up to 40+%) due to higher frequency measurements and measurement board sweeps. Basically in the upcoming plots, don't compare these numbers directly against the snow report; the results are meant to be percentages of normal.

Scatter plot of El Niño vs. La Niña Snowfall

Over the past 76 winters, on average, seasonal snowfall decreases by about 11 inches per +1 °C of winter ONI at Bridger, the measure of El Nino's strength (more positive = stronger El Niño, more negative = stronger La Niña, -0.5–0.5 = neutral). It's important to note that despite the relationship, ENSO explains only part of the year-to-year variance. It does, however, in this case load the dice against us.

What's interesting to me is looking at where the loss is most prominent. In the plot you can see that the trend is steeper at the top of the range than the bottom: the biggest winters see a decrease of about 16″ per °C of El Niño, the driest about 5–6″. This indicates to me that while El Nino generally means less snow across the board, its bigger effect is on capping the ceiling. None of the eight strong El Niño winters since 1950 cleared 200 inches, while half of the strong La Niña winters did. Furthermore, though not shown here, looking at Bridger's top-20 biggest storm cycles on record, 11 landed in La Niña winters and just 5 in El Niño winters. TLDR is La Niña winters skew above normal in terms of snowfall ~2/3rds of the time, whereas zero of the eight historical El Niño winters had any more than a few inches above average.

Mean seasonal totals are 143″ for a strong El Niño → 158″ for neutral ENSO → 186″ for strong La Niña, compared with a 164″ climatological mean. You're probably asking what happened last year, wasn't that a La Niña? Sort of. ENSO quickly flipped to neutral early in the season, technically making it not a La Niña winter at least by these metrics.

Why El Niño's Pattern = Less Snowfall

If we composite 76 winters of reanalysis fields, the pattern during strong El Niño's mid-winter has a deeper Aleutian low (dark blues off the Pacific NW) and also have more prominent ridging over western Canada to the northern Rockies over MT (notice the lines look like they form a mountain ridge with redder colors). This coincides with a storm track that tends to split and provides California with more precipitation than typical winters. Strong La Niña's, on the other hand, feature a North Pacific ridge and a trough digging into the Northwest, which leads to a favorable storm track from the W/NW for us.

Is there any good news in all of this? Well, Bozeman-area station records, reanalysis, and SNOTEL all seem to indicate that strong El Niño winters here are not reliably warmer with differences of only 0.1–0.6 °C. This result actually surprised me a bit. Historically, the warmest stretches globally come a few months after a big El Niño peaks, which is typically late winter into spring. The year after previous major events (1998, 2016, 2024) have tended to set a new global temperature record, however, that signal seems much weaker for our local climatology.

So what does 2026–27 look like?

Our three very-strong analog winters (DJF ONI ≥ 2.0) are 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16, which had 167″, 112″, and 138″ at Bridger respectively (remember these are the snotel numbers and would correspond to ~ 233, 157, and 193" for Bridger's direct measurements). This is a pretty wide spread and ranges anywhere from a decent winter near average to a dry one similar to last season. So here are what the numbers are telling me in summary: ~80–90% chance of finishing below the climo mean, and only ~10–15% chance of an above average season (*insert Jim Carrey meme*). Basically, I'd suggest tempering expectations, but I don't think all hope is lost!

A couple of disclaimers:

  • The strongest winter ENSO in the record is 2015-16 at +2.63, and this year's forecast sits there or above. If the El Niño is above CPC's historic threshold, we don't have anything to compare it to.
  • ENSO still explains only part of a winter here in SW MT. The other parts are the polar jet, storm luck, and whatever the North Pacific decides in February. 1982-83 was a big time El Niño and was still near climatology.

What about Big Sky?

The story is pretty similar down the road at Big Sky. The record there for the Lone Mountain Snotel is shorter (only goes back to 1992), but the ENSO relationship is, if anything, a touch stronger: about 14 inches lost per +1 °C of winter ONI, and the relationship explains a larger share of the variance than at Bridger.

Compared to a normal of about 141 inches at Lone Mountain, the strong-El-Niño winters on record averaged roughly 114″ (about 80% of normal); however, the two closest very-strong analogs, 1997-98 and 2015-16, both were near 95%.

Bottom line

Expect fewer big storm days, but I wouldn't completely write off the season.

The snow that does fall should still be cold, since there's no reliable temperature signal here with El Nino, and it all comes down to the storm track.

CPC's next update is on October 8. I'll continue to provide updates leading into the season.

Pray for snow. And taking a quick peek at the forecast for next weekend we may have our first ❄️ to discuss! More soon and thanks for reading!

-Trey

*Methods: DJF Oceanic Niño Index (CPC), 76 usable Bridger seasons (Nov–Apr totals) from the Brackett Creek SNOTEL record (extended to 1950 with the nearby co-op station). Composites are reanalysis anomalies. The 2026-27 outlook centers on a forecast ONI of +2.9 (ranging 2.6–3.2) and CPC's >90% very-strong probability. ENSO status from the CPC ENSO Diagnostic Discussion issued 2026-09-10 and CPC's weekly update of 2026-09-28.*
